definitions.definition: u_t(x,t)=∂u(x,t)/∂t, component by component. Derivatives are the usual real derivatives; a derivative not existing is assigned the total derivative convention value zero. When u is smooth on its open domain these are classical derivatives.
u_tt(x,t)=∂u_t(x,t)/∂t, component by component, with the same total derivative convention.

definitions.type: family indexed by j∈{1,…,n} of maps ℝ^n × (0,∞) → ℝ^m
definitions.definition: u_j(j,x,t)=∂_{x_j}u(x,t), the derivative along the jth standard coordinate direction, component by component with the total derivative convention. We also write u_j when the index j is explicitly fixed.

definitions.type: family indexed by j∈{1,…,n} of maps ℝ^n × (0,∞) → ℝ^m
definitions.definition: u_jj(j,x,t)=∂_{x_j}u_j(j,x,t), with the total derivative convention. The notation u_jj with fixed j has this same meaning.

definitions.type: family indexed by j∈{1,…,n} of maps ℝ^n × (0,∞) → ℝ^m
definitions.definition: v_j(j,x,t)=∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t), with the total derivative convention. With fixed j we abbreviate this by v_j.
Δu(x,t)=∑_{j=1}^n u_jj(j,x,t), the componentwise spatial Laplacian Δ_xu of the input.

e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|²+∑_{j=1}^n |u_j(j,x,t)|². Here |z|²=z·z is the Euclidean norm square on ℝ^m, so the spatial sum is exactly the Frobenius square |Du|². All integrals in the proof are Lebesgue integrals, and dx denotes standard volume on ℝ^n.
e_t(x,t)=∂e(x,t)/∂t, using the total derivative convention, whose classical existence and formula will be proved.

inputs.statement: Let K be a nontrivially normed field and V,W normed additive commutative groups and normed K-spaces. Let f:V→W, z∈V, and k∈ℕ∞ω. output.statement: n≥1 and m≥1. The map u and all its partial derivatives are smooth on ℝ^n×(0,∞); in particular ∂_t u_j(j,x,t)=v_j(j,x,t) and e_t(x,t)=2u_t(x,t)·u_tt(x,t)+2∑_{j=1}^n u_j(j,x,t)·v_j(j,x,t). For every t0>0, let J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. There exist a compact C⊆ℝ^n and R>0 such that C⊆(−R,R)^n, u(x,r)=q for x∉C and r∈J, and every positive-order derivative of u vanishes for x∉C and r∈int J. Put Q=[−R,R]^n, whose Lebesgue measure is (2R)^n. For every r∈int J the following scalar spatial functions are continuous, zero outside C, and Lebesgue integrable: e(·,r), e_t(·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_tt(·,r), and, for each j, u_j(j,·,r)·v_j(j,·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_jj(j,·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_j(j,·,r), and ∂_{x_j}(u_t(·,r)·u_j(j,·,r)). Their absolute integrals are finite, each bounded by a finite supremum on Q times (2R)^n. In particular e(·,t) is integrable for every t>0.

locals.declaration: Choose C with the common support property in F001.
Choose R>0 with C⊆(−R,R)^n from F002.

argument.text: H001 supplies n,m≥1. Fix t0>0 and J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. The endpoints satisfy 0<t0/2<3t0/2, so H006 gives a compact spatial set common to all times in J. Separately, H002 ensures that all partial derivatives of u are smooth on the open domain. M007 over ℝ at each point, applied to the spatial and time coordinate vectors, gives ∂_t u_j=v_j. The input is locally smooth at that point, so it is in particular C² there; if a total ambient map is needed, extend u by zero off the positive-time domain, which leaves it smooth on a neighborhood of the point. Differentiating each squared norm using M006, and the finite-sum differentiation rule, therefore gives e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2∑_j u_j·v_j throughout the domain. These formulas also show e and e_t are smooth.

produces.statement: There exists a compact C0⊆ℝ^n such that u(y,r)=q for every y∉C0 and r∈J.
All partial derivatives of u are smooth on the open positive-time domain; ∂_t u_j=v_j and e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2∑_{j=1}^n u_j·v_j at every point. The functions e and e_t are smooth there.

argument.text: Choose C from F001. Apply M008 on C to the identity map into Euclidean ℝ^n. It gives a finite real bound on |x| for x∈C. Increase this bound, if necessary, to a positive R larger than it. Since |x_j|≤|x|, C⊆(−R,R)^n. Thus such a positive R exists, even if C is empty.

produces.statement: There exists R0>0 such that C⊆(−R0,R0)^n.

argument.text: Choose R from F002 and set Q=[−R,R]^n. This closed box is compact, measurable, and has finite Lebesgue measure (2R)^n. The compact set C is closed in ℝ^n. On the open set (ℝ^n\C)×int J, F001 says u=q. At every point of this open set u is constant in a neighborhood; differentiating the constant on that neighborhood, successively in each coordinate, gives zero for every positive-order derivative. Consequently at any r∈int J e, e_t, u_t·u_tt, and for each spatial index the functions u_j·v_j, u_t·u_jj, u_t·u_j, and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·u_j) vanish outside C: every summand contains such a derivative. For the last function, the product rule expands it into v_j·u_j+u_t·u_jj, both of which vanish there. Continuity and smoothness follow from F003 and smoothness of the dot product.

produces.statement: C⊆int Q, and Q is compact and measurable with finite Lebesgue measure (2R)^n. For every r∈int J, the spatial functions e(·,r), e_t(·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_tt(·,r), and, for every j∈{1,…,n}, u_j(j,·,r)·v_j(j,·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_jj(j,·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_j(j,·,r), and ∂_{x_j}(u_t(·,r)·u_j(j,·,r)) are continuous and vanish outside C. Their nonzero sets therefore have closures contained in the compact set C.

argument.text: For every r∈int J apply M005 to each continuous scalar function in F004, on ℝ^n with Lebesgue measure. Its support closure is a closed subset of compact C, hence compact; Lebesgue measure is finite on compact sets. Each is therefore integrable. Equivalently its norm is bounded on Q by M008 and it vanishes outside Q, so its absolute integral is at most that finite bound times |Q|=(2R)^n. This also supplies the stated finiteness estimate for all terms. Since t0 belongs to int J, e(·,t0) is integrable. As t0 was arbitrary, this holds at every positive time. Together with F003 and F004 this proves the complete common-support and integrability statement, including the common support witnesses and all derivative-product integrability assertions.
